lessons.title: Values, slices and numbers
lessons.intro: Most Python surprises in interviews come from three places: what a name refers to, how slices and sorting behave, and how numbers round. Learn the rules once and they stop being surprises.
takeaways: Slices do not raise on bad bounds.
Sorting is stable; use it for multi-key ordering.
Floor division and banker's rounding are not C++ behaviour.
lessons.trap: Using `int(a / b)` to emulate C++ division is wrong for large integers because it goes through floating point. Use `a // b` with care for negatives, or `divmod`.

sections.heading: Slices are forgiving
sections.text: `s[a:b:c]` never raises for out-of-range bounds, and a negative step walks backwards. That is handy for reversing (`s[::-1]`) and risky when an off-by-one hides.

sections.heading: Sorting is stable
sections.text: `sorted` and `list.sort` keep the original order of items with equal keys. To order by several criteria, sort by the least important key first, or return a tuple from `key`.

sections.heading: Integer division and rounding
sections.text: `//` floors toward negative infinity and `%` takes the sign of the divisor. `round` sends ties to the nearest even number. Both differ from C++ truncation, which matters when you port a solution between the two languages.

lessons.title: Comprehensions and generators
lessons.intro: A comprehension builds a whole collection now. A generator produces values one at a time, on demand. Choosing between them is a memory and laziness decision.
takeaways: Use a comprehension when you need the whole collection.
Use a generator for streams and single passes.
A generator can be consumed only once.
lessons.trap: Calling `len()` on a generator fails, and `sum(g)` twice returns the right answer the first time and 0 the second.

sections.heading: Comprehensions
sections.text: They read as 'for each x, keep f(x)'. The same syntax builds lists, sets and dicts. Keep them to one loop and one condition; past that, a plain loop is clearer.
code: print({w: len(w) for w in set(words) if len(w) > 2})

sections.heading: Generators are one-shot
sections.text: A generator expression yields each value once, then it is exhausted. Reusing it silently gives nothing, which is a classic source of 'my second pass is empty' bugs.
code: g = (x * x for x in range(4))

sections.heading: Why bother
sections.text: Streaming a large file or a long training set through a generator keeps memory flat. `yield` lets you write the producer as an ordinary loop.
code: for i in range(0, len(xs), n):

lessons.title: Closures, decorators and functools
lessons.intro: Functions are values. A function can capture variables from where it was defined, and a decorator is a function that wraps another function.
takeaways: A closure sees the variable at call time.
Always use `functools.wraps` in decorators.
`lru_cache` needs hashable arguments and unbounded caches grow forever.
lessons.trap: Caching a function that takes a list or a numpy array raises `TypeError: unhashable`. Cache on a tuple or an id instead.

sections.heading: Closures capture variables, not values
sections.text: A closure looks the variable up when it runs. Lambdas created in a loop all see the loop variable's final value unless you bind it, for example with a default argument.
code: fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]

sections.heading: Decorators wrap
sections.text: `@deco` above `def f` means `f = deco(f)`. Use `functools.wraps` so the wrapper keeps the name and docstring.

sections.heading: Memoisation
sections.text: `functools.lru_cache` stores results keyed by the arguments, which must be hashable. It turns exponential recursion into linear time, at the price of memory.
code: return n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

lessons.title: Aliasing and copies
lessons.intro: Assignment never copies. It makes another name for the same object. Whether a change is visible through the other name depends on whether the object is mutable and whether the operation mutates it.
takeaways: Assignment shares; it does not copy.
A shallow copy shares nested objects.
Build 2-D grids with a comprehension.
lessons.trap: numpy slices are views, not copies: writing into a slice changes the original array. Use `.copy()` when you need independence (see the numpy lessons).

sections.heading: Two names, one list
sections.text: `b = a` binds a second name. Mutating through either shows through both.

sections.heading: Shallow versus deep
sections.text: `a.copy()` and `a[:]` copy only the outer list; the inner objects are shared. `copy.deepcopy` copies recursively.

sections.heading: The grid trap
sections.text: `[[0] * 3] * 3` repeats one inner list three times. Build each row separately.

lessons.title: Collections and what they cost
lessons.intro: Interview Python is mostly about picking the right container and knowing its cost. The standard library already has most of what you would otherwise hand-roll.
takeaways: Pick the container for the operation you repeat.
Know the O(1) versus O(n) list operations.
A set or dict is the default for membership.
lessons.trap: Dictionaries preserve insertion order, but sets do not promise any order. Never rely on set iteration order in an answer.

sections.heading: Counter, defaultdict, deque
sections.text: `Counter` counts, `defaultdict` creates missing values on first access, and `deque` gives O(1) operations at both ends.
code: from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque

sections.heading: Costs worth memorising
sections.text: Appending to a list and indexing are O(1). `list.pop(0)` and `list.insert(0, x)` are O(n). `x in list` is O(n); `x in set` and `x in dict` are average O(1). Sorting is O(n log n). String `+=` in a loop can be O(n²) while `''.join` is linear.

sections.heading: A cheap fix with a big effect
sections.text: Converting a list you search repeatedly into a set is often the whole optimisation.

lessons.title: heapq, bisect and itertools
lessons.intro: Three small modules cover a large share of coding-round patterns: priority queues, binary search on sorted lists, and iteration helpers.
takeaways: Min-heap by default; negate for max.
bisect needs a sorted list.
groupby only merges neighbours.
lessons.trap: Heap entries that tie on priority fall through to comparing the next tuple element. Add a counter as a tiebreaker when the payloads cannot be compared.

sections.heading: heapq is a min-heap on a list
sections.text: `heappush` and `heappop` cost O(log n). For a max-heap push negated values. `nlargest(k, xs)` is O(n log k).

sections.heading: bisect for sorted lists
sections.text: `bisect_left` returns the first insertion point and `bisect_right` the one after equal items. Their difference counts equal elements.

sections.heading: itertools
sections.text: `accumulate` gives prefix sums, `groupby` groups consecutive equal keys (sort first to group everything), `combinations` and `permutations` enumerate subsets lazily.

lessons.title: Context managers and exceptions
lessons.intro: Resources must be released even when code fails. `with` and `try`/`finally` are Python's RAII.
takeaways: Use `with` for files, locks and temporary state.
Catch narrow, re-raise with context.
Never return from `finally`.
lessons.trap: Returning True from `__exit__` swallows the exception. That is occasionally right and usually a hidden bug.

sections.heading: with
sections.text: `__enter__` runs on the way in and `__exit__` always runs on the way out, even when an exception escapes. `contextlib.contextmanager` writes one as a generator.

sections.heading: Catch narrowly
sections.text: Catch the specific exception you can handle. A bare `except:` also hides `KeyboardInterrupt` and typos. Use `raise ... from err` to keep the cause chain.

sections.heading: finally wins
sections.text: Code in `finally` runs last, and a `return` there overrides everything before it. Do not return from `finally`.

lessons.title: Dataclasses and type hints
lessons.intro: Dataclasses remove boilerplate for plain data records, and type hints document intent for people and tools. Neither changes what the interpreter does at run time.
takeaways: Use dataclasses for records.
`default_factory` for mutable defaults.
Type hints are for tools and readers, not for the runtime.
lessons.trap: A dataclass with `eq=True` and no `frozen` sets `__hash__` to None, so it cannot go in a set or be a dict key.

sections.heading: Dataclasses
sections.text: `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from annotated fields. Mutable defaults need `field(default_factory=...)`. `frozen=True` makes instances hashable and read-only.

sections.heading: Hints are not enforced
sections.text: Python stores annotations and ignores them. Static checkers (mypy, pyright) and libraries that opt in (pydantic) use them. Annotate public signatures; it pays off in review and in AI-assisted coding.

lessons.title: Recursion and its limits
lessons.intro: Python does not optimise tail calls and caps the stack. Deep recursion is a design choice you make knowingly.
takeaways: Expect RecursionError near 1000 frames.
Prefer an explicit stack for deep inputs.
Memoisation does not shorten the call chain.
lessons.trap: In an interview say the limit out loud and offer the iterative version when inputs can be a long chain.

sections.heading: The limit
sections.text: CPython allows about a thousand nested calls by default. Raising the limit trades a clean error for the risk of crashing the interpreter.

sections.heading: Replace depth with a stack
sections.text: Any recursive DFS can use an explicit stack, which lives on the heap and has no fixed ceiling.
code: chain = {i: i + 1 for i in range(5000)}

lessons.title: Testing numerical code
lessons.intro: A test that cannot fail is not a test, and floating-point equality is the quickest way to write one that fails for the wrong reason.
takeaways: Never compare floats with `==`.
Finite differences verify gradients.
Test the failing case first.
lessons.trap: Choosing h too small makes the difference dominated by rounding error; 1e-5 to 1e-6 is a good range in float64.

sections.heading: Compare with tolerance
sections.text: Use `pytest.approx` or `math.isclose` for floats. Pick the tolerance from the problem, not from what makes the test pass.

sections.heading: Check a gradient numerically
sections.text: A central difference `(f(x+h) - f(x-h)) / 2h` approximates the derivative to O(h²). Neural Clash labs use it to verify every hand-written gradient.
